strengths: Compelling end-to-end differentiable formulation that unifies feed-forward multi-view 3D Gaussian reconstruction (MVSplat), transformer-based particle dynamics, and 3DGS rendering supervised solely by image reconstruction loss.

Clever adaptation of Point Transformer v3 (PTv3) to spatiotemporal dynamics via temporally serialized space-filling curves (t-SPC) and temporal merging, which avoids the computational bottleneck of kNN graph construction and FPS prevalent in GNN-based particle simulators.
Comprehensive ablation study covering rollout lengths, explicit vs. latent dynamics representations, temporal merging strides, grid resolutions, and camera requirements.

Interesting emergent behaviors enabled by the 3D representation, such as zero-shot multi-body composition, interactive scene editing (e.g., removing the ground or altering drop height), and shadow consistency.
Near real-time inference speed (16–20 FPS on an H100) and commitment to open-source code and benchmark datasets.
weaknesses: Baselines are primarily limited to 2D video generation (Cosmos / CosmosFT). While the lack of public code/data for 3D visuo-physical baselines (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL) is noted, the paper does not benchmark against an adapted GNN-based particle baseline on the same representation to empirically isolate the benefits of the proposed SFC-transformer dynamics engine over standard GNNs.

Evaluation is restricted to synthetic simulation environments (Genesis MPM and GSO objects) with simple flat grounds and drop trajectories across a small set of objects (6 objects per domain); real-world video verification is absent.

High sensitivity to multi-view camera coverage: the method relies on multi-view video inputs (4 input views + 5 target views), and performance drops substantially when view counts are reduced (failing completely on 2 views out of 4).

Minor presentation errors in the manuscript: on page 8, the text cites 'Table 11' for hyperparameter ablations, but the corresponding table on page 8 is incorrectly titled 'Figure 11' (and the detailed ablation tables are in the Appendix as Tables S1–S6).

strengths: End-to-end differentiable design: 3DGSim seamlessly integrates feed-forward multi-view 3D Gaussian Splatting (extending MVSplat) with a transformer dynamics engine and differentiable rasterization, removing the need for privileged 3D particle tracks or depth supervision.

Efficient dynamics modeling without kNN graphs: By extending Point Transformer v3 (PTv3) with space-filling curves (SFC) and temporal merging via bit-shifting, the framework bypasses expensive kNN graph construction and radius searches, allowing near real-time inference (16–20 FPS).

Effective handling of diverse physics: The model successfully demonstrates learning across distinct physical regimes—rigid bodies, elastoplastic deformation, and constrained cloth dynamics—using only image reconstruction losses (L2 + LPIPS).

Strong 3D composability and scene editability: Due to the explicit 3D particle state representation, the model natively supports counterfactual edits such as ground plane manipulation, novel object combinations, and multi-body interactions without retraining.
Thorough ablation study: The appendix provides extensive and insightful ablations on temporal merger schedules, grid resolutions, camera setups, and training rollout horizons.
weaknesses: Absence of particle-based 3D baselines: While the paper notes the lack of public code/data for methods like VPD, HD-VPD, and DEL, comparing quantitatively only against a 2D generative video model (Cosmos) makes it harder to isolate the specific advantage of the proposed transformer + SFC formulation over a standard GNN-based 3D dynamics baseline on the same dataset.

Reliance on multi-view calibrated cameras and synthetic scenes: The framework requires multiple calibrated, synchronized viewpoints (defaulting to 4 input and 5 target views) and is evaluated exclusively on synthetic simulators (Genesis MPM and GSO assets with clean backgrounds). Real-world capture remains unvalidated.

Physical artifacts in complex out-of-distribution compositions: As acknowledged in Figure 10, when scaling to heavier multi-body compositions, the learned dynamics suffer from penetration artifacts (e.g., objects penetrating the support plane and leaking particles), revealing the limitations of purely unconstrained learned priors without explicit contact handling.

strengths: The paper presents an elegant, fully differentiable end-to-end framework (3DGSim) combining feed-forward multi-view 3D Gaussian reconstruction (MVSplat), point transformer dynamics (PTv3), and Gaussian Splatting rendering supervised purely by RGB reconstruction.

Replacing costly kNN graph construction with space-filling curve serialization and patch-based attention provides a scalable alternative to traditional GNN particle simulators, achieving near real-time inference speed (16–20 FPS).
The supplementary material includes detailed ablation studies covering rollout length, camera viewpoints, background masking, grid resolution, and temporal merging schedules.
Qualitative demonstrations showcase appealing capabilities including novel view synthesis, shadow prediction, and basic scene editability (such as ground removal and multi-object duplication).
weaknesses: Absence of particle/3D dynamics baselines: The paper does not benchmark against any existing 3D particle-based or NeRF-based simulators (e.g., VPD, HD-VPD, DEL, 3D-IntPhys, or DPI-Net adapted to point clouds). The only quantitative comparison is against Cosmos, a 2D autoregressive video generation model, which operates under very different assumptions and is inherently disadvantaged on multi-view 3D consistency metrics.

Evaluation relies solely on 2D image quality metrics: Despite generating trajectories from analytical simulators (Genesis MPM, rigid body engine) where ground-truth 3D geometry and motion states are available, the paper does not report any physical or 3D geometric metrics (e.g., 3D Chamfer Distance, Earth Mover's Distance, center-of-mass trajectory error, or collision penetration). Evaluating physical simulators purely via PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS masks potential 3D physical inaccuracies.

Limited dataset scale and diversity: Experiments are conducted exclusively on synthetic datasets with simple object geometries (only 6 objects per category: rigid, elastic, cloth) falling onto planar surfaces with clean backgrounds, without real-world video validation.

Dependence on dense multi-view calibrated setups: The method requires synchronized and calibrated multi-view camera inputs (typically 9 to 12 camera views during training). Appendix B.2 demonstrates that reducing the setup to sparse views (e.g., 2 views out of 4) fails completely, which significantly restricts applicability to real-world scenarios.
Minor presentation errors: In Section 5.1, the text refers to 'Table 11' and 'Figure 11' interchangeably, where Figure 11 is structured as a quantitative table.

strengths: Compelling end-to-end formulation: The paper effectively integrates feed-forward multi-view inverse rendering (MVSplat), an efficient transformer-based point dynamics engine (PTv3 with novel temporal serialization and merging), and differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting into a unified framework trained solely on RGB video reconstruction losses.

Elimination of expensive kNN graph operations: Adapting space-filling curves and patch-wise attention (TEM + PTv3) to dynamic point clouds overcomes the quadratic/expensive neighbor search and fixed-horizon limitations of traditional GNN-based particle simulators, achieving near real-time inference (~16–20 FPS).

Strong physical generalization and scene editability: By grounding dynamics in a 3D particle state rather than 2D pixel space, 3DGSim exhibits impressive out-of-distribution generalization—such as ground removal, higher release heights, and multi-object collisions—where state-of-the-art 2D video models (CosmosFT) fail by hallucinating levitation or merging separate bodies.

Comprehensive evaluation and ablations: The manuscript is thoroughly ablated across temporal merging strategies, latent vs. explicit representations, rollout lengths, grid sizes, camera densities, and includes preliminary real-world testing on the HO-Cap dataset.
weaknesses: Reliance on multi-view calibration: The primary framework depends heavily on calibrated multi-view camera setups (4–12 views), which limits its immediate applicability to widely available in-the-wild monocular video domains, despite the preliminary monocular depth adaptation on HO-Cap.

Autoregressive drift and particle fading over long horizons: As acknowledged in the failure analysis (Figure S15), long-horizon autoregressive rollouts (e.g., beyond 4 seconds) suffer from error accumulation, resulting in particle drift, loss of high-frequency detail, or fading transparency.

Limited complexity of synthetic benchmarks: While three physical regimes (rigid, elastic, cloth) are investigated, the scenarios are relatively constrained (single objects dropping onto flat grounds or corner-pinned cloths with 6 object meshes per domain).

Baseline comparisons: Direct quantitative comparisons against other learned 3D particle-from-video models (such as VPD or DEL) are missing due to closed-source implementations, leaving Spring-Gaus (an analytical per-scene optimizer) and 2D Cosmos as the main baselines.

strengths: Principled and fully differentiable end-to-end design: The paper cleanly integrates feed-forward multi-view reconstruction (MVSplat/DepthAnything3), an efficient transformer-based particle dynamics engine, and differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting, training solely on multi-view RGB video reconstruction without requiring ground-truth particle supervision or depth sensors.

Efficient dynamics formulation: By extending Point Transformer v3 (PTv3) with space-filling curve serialization and a novel Temporal Encoding and Merging (TEM) module, the method circumvents expensive kNN graph constructions and FPS downsampling typical of GNN-based particle simulators, achieving near real-time rollout speeds (~16-20 FPS).

Detailed ablation study: The experiments systematically evaluate key design choices—including temporal merging strategies, latent vs. explicit Gaussian state parameterizations, rollout training lengths, grid resolution, and camera density—clearly demonstrating the necessity of the proposed components.

Demonstration of physical inductive bias and spatial causality: Qualitative tests on zero-shot out-of-distribution scenarios (ground removal, multi-body interactions from single-body training, and drop height variations) demonstrate that the explicit 3D formulation avoids common generative artifacts of 2D video models (e.g., CosmosFT hallucinating floating objects or merging distinct bodies).
weaknesses: Evaluation relies strictly on image-space metrics: Although Section E argues that learned particles do not directly correspond to underlying simulation particles, the lack of explicit 3D geometric or trajectory evaluation (e.g., Chamfer distance, center-of-mass tracking, or collision error against simulator ground truth) makes it difficult to quantitatively isolate physical accuracy from novel-view rendering quality.

Limited benchmarking against 3D learned physics baselines: While the authors note that prior 3D visuo-physical baselines (such as VPD, HD-VPD, and DEL) have not released open-source implementations or datasets, comparing primarily against a 2D generative video baseline (Cosmos) and an analytical spring-mass model (Spring-Gauss) leaves a gap in comparing against competitive learned particle/neural-field simulators under identical settings.

Simplicity of synthetic environments and autoregressive degradation: Synthetic evaluation is confined to simple tabletop-like settings with single colored objects dropping onto circular platforms or fixed cloths with plain backgrounds. Furthermore, as shown in the real-world manipulation rollout (Figure S15), autoregressive rollouts suffer from particle dissipation, blurring, and loss of actuation over longer temporal horizons.

Multi-view and camera calibration dependence: The primary pipeline depends on calibrated multi-view camera rigs (up to 12 cameras during training). While the preliminary HO-Cap experiment adapts a monocular depth prior, fully relaxing multi-view requirements remains an open challenge for real-world scaling.

strengths: Principled and scalable architecture: The paper successfully integrates feed-forward multi-view 3D reconstruction (MVSplat), an efficient transformer dynamics model (extending PTv3), and differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) into an end-to-end framework trained purely via video reconstruction loss without requiring ground-truth particle supervision.

Efficient temporal dynamics formulation: Replacing traditional kNN graph constructions and furthest-point-sampling with space-filling curve serialization and hierarchical Temporal Encoding & Merging (TEM) significantly reduces computational complexity, enabling near real-time simulation speeds (16–20 FPS).

Superior physical grounding and zero-shot generalization over 2D models: The model demonstrates clear spatial causality and object permanence under scene edits (e.g., ground plane removal, variable drop heights, and multi-object collisions despite being trained on single-body data), where state-of-the-art 2D video models (Cosmos) fail and exhibit severe hallucinations or identity collapse.

Thorough ablation studies: The paper provides extensive and well-isolated ablation experiments verifying the necessity of the TEM module, latent vs. explicit Gaussian representations, rollout horizons, and grid pooling resolutions.
weaknesses: Evaluation restricted primarily to simple synthetic setups: The core experiments are performed on simulated trajectories featuring isolated objects from a small set of 6 CAD models dropping onto a ground plane or cloth. The real-world results on HO-Cap are preliminary, rely on external DepthAnything3 features and 3D hand keypoints, and exhibit particle dissipation over longer rollouts.

Limited 3D learned baselines: While the authors reasonably justify the difficulty of benchmarking against closed-source works (VPD, HD-VPD, DEL), the quantitative baselines are mostly restricted to a 2D foundation model (Cosmos) and an analytical spring-mass model (Spring-Gauss) rather than modern learned particle-based world models.

Lack of direct 3D geometric/physical metric evaluation: Although Section E defends image-space metrics due to differences between visual Gaussians and simulation particles, image-based metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) can be insensitive to subtle physical violations or hidden geometry. Ground-truth 3D evaluation (e.g., Chamfer Distance or center-of-mass tracking error) on synthetic test sets would significantly strengthen the physical validation.

Dependence on dense multi-view coverage: As detailed in the ablation on camera setup (Section C.2), performance degrades substantially when camera views are reduced (e.g., dropping to 2–3 views causes training failures or planar collapse), limiting immediate applicability to sparse or monocular real-world settings.
